<reason>B built the more coherent and durable theory of the motion: disclosure informs only when it discriminates or is substantive, and the universal bare notice the motion mandates is neither. B defused A's "self-refutation" trilemma by showing obvious/expensive/dangerous attach to three different versions of the right, turned A's nutrition-label and sponsored-tag analogies against the scoped-down right A disavowed in A1.6, and gave a precise account of why adverse-action notices work (specific decision, named reasons, attached levers) that the dating banner lacks. B also landed an unanswered offensive point: machine-blame is exactly what boost purchases promise to fix, so A's central harm is plausibly worsened, not cured. A's "door/floor" framing was never cashed out — B showed enforcement never needed admissions and no app claims an "organic pool," gutting A4.1's named complaint. A's closing victory claim over B4.3 was spin (B's named disclosures all satisfy the discrimination principle), and B5.1's quote-back of A5.3 was the debate's kill shot: the fact A wants users to have is the substantive one A disavowed. Both sides were disciplined, polished, and format-compliant; both had clipped turns, with B's extra clip a minor cost that does not offset the argumentative gap.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 sequence B2.1–B2.5: recasting the "contradiction" as a fork across three versions of the right, then showing A's nutrition-facts and sponsored-content analogies describe discriminating, substantive labels — the very disclosure A1.6 refused to defend — capped by "a signal that's always on is not a signal." That framework absorbed A's best pressure for the rest of the debate and powered B5.1's closing reversal.</best_rebuttal>
